name: Late Julian apples
why_now: September's apples were for eating raw. October's are Julian's late ones — Granny Smith, Pink Lady, Winesap — tarter and firmer, which is exactly what you want in a hot pan. They hold their shape next to pork instead of turning to sauce.
how_to_choose: Firm, with no give near the stem
Tart varieties for the pan; sweeter ones for eating
The blossom end should smell like apple
Ask which ones hold up to heat
buy_this_much: 4–6. Two for the pan, the rest for eating. Buy them weekly; crisp is the point.
price_note: Julian's orchards thin out by the end of the month. Buy them early if you're driving up.

flavor_paths.name: In the pan
flavor_paths.description: Wedges into the fat after a pork chop, a splash of cider vinegar. Now you cook them.

flavor_paths.name: Shredded
flavor_paths.description: A slaw with cider vinegar and pomegranate.

flavor_paths.name: Raw and cold
flavor_paths.description: With sharp cheddar. Still the best way to eat half of them.

weekday_uses: In the pan after pork chops, with sage
Sliced thin into a slaw with pomegranate
weekend_use: Thick wedges browned in butter and served warm with a spoonful of yogurt — the only dessert October needs.
storage: In the fridge, away from anything that absorbs smells. Cold, they stay crisp for weeks.
one_thing_to_learn: A cooking apple is just a tart, firm one. Sugar makes an apple collapse under heat; acid and density hold it together. That's why September said don't bake them yet, and October says go ahead.
market_question: Which of these holds up in a pan?
